## 2

I get the instinct to question authority and not accept official images at face value—healthy skepticism is fine. But the Earth being round doesn't depend on NASA, modern governments, or digital photographs. People figured it out thousands of years ago using simple geometry and observations anyone can test.

For instance, Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference around 240 BCE simply by measuring the shadows cast by sticks in two different cities on the same day. You can also see the curvature yourself: ships don't just shrink as they sail away, they sink hull-first below the horizon. During every lunar eclipse, the shadow the Earth casts on the Moon is curved, which only a sphere consistently produces from every angle. Plus, if you travel south of the equator, you see entirely different constellations that are physically impossible to view from the north.

To believe the Earth is flat, you’d have to accept that millions of commercial pilots, ship navigators, amateur astronomers, and competing world governments spanning centuries are all actively maintaining a massive, unbroken conspiracy—with no real motive. At a certain point, the physics simply make much more sense than the conspiracy.

## 3

Think of sunlight as a package deal. Even though it looks white or clear to us, it’s actually made of every color of the rainbow mixed together. Each color travels as a wave, but they don't all look the same: red and orange have long, lazy waves, while blue and violet have short, choppy waves.

When sunlight hits Earth's atmosphere, it enters a thick blanket of air filled with tiny gas molecules like nitrogen and oxygen. The long, lazy red and yellow waves pass right through those tiny molecules without bumping into them much. But the short, choppy blue waves smack right into the gas molecules and bounce off in every direction. 

Scientists call this **scattering**. While the rest of the sunlight beams straight down to the ground, that scattered blue light gets tossed all over the atmosphere like a pinball. When you look up at the daytime sky away from the Sun, you’re looking at that scattered blue light reaching your eyes from every angle.

(And if you're wondering why it’s blue instead of violet, since violet waves are even shorter: the Sun produces way more blue light than violet light, and our human eyes are much better at seeing blue!)
